scenes.headline: How Haru listens and talks at the same time
scenes.sub: One model, three streams, one 133 ms clock
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Pippa! Haru is an open full-duplex speech model from a Japanese startup. Let's see how one model listens and talks at once.

scenes.title: Why voice pipelines wait
scenes.sub: Four models in a relay, one floor
scenes.say: Chapter one. Why voice pipelines wait.

scenes.title: The usual voice assistant
scenes.say: Most voice assistants are a relay of four models.

items.say: First, a detector waits until you have been quiet long enough to be sure you finished.
Then speech recognition writes down what you said. Your laugh and your tone stay behind.
A text model writes the answer.
And a speech synthesiser reads it out. Every stage waits for the one before.

left.title: Cascade
items: A backchannel looks like an interruption
left.say: In a relay, only one side holds the floor, and a polite mm-hm looks exactly like an interruption.

right.title: Full-duplex
right.say: A full-duplex model drops the floor. It hears and speaks every frame, and overlap is just more data.

scenes.title: Three streams, one clock
scenes.say: Chapter two. Three streams, one clock.

scenes.text: Every 133 ms, add your audio, the model's own audio and its text into a single position of one language model.
scenes.say: Here's the idea. Every frame, add your audio, the model's own audio, and its text into a single position of one language model.

legend: The clock never stops: one frame in, one frame out
A backchannel is just audio on your row
An interruption: it trails off a couple of frames in

steps.term: EOP: the token before it starts speaking
steps.say: Time runs in frames of a hundred and thirty-three milliseconds. You ask. The model writes padding, then an end-of-padding token, and starts to speak.
Take one frame. Your audio, its own audio and its text token are added into one position. The output predicts the next text token and the next audio.
Now you say mm-hm while it talks. That is just sound on your row. Trained on real overlapping speech, it keeps going.
Interrupt it properly, and it should trail off a couple of frames in, the way people do in the recordings it learned from.
Summing matters. Six frames interleaved would take eighteen positions. Summed, they take six.
The company's own figure. Interleaving puts user audio, text and model audio in separate positions, one after another.
Haru stacks them. Three tokens share one position per frame, and the next text and audio come out together.

scenes.title: Audio as one vector
scenes.sub: Continuous latents and a one-step head
scenes.say: Chapter three. Audio as one vector.

steps.term: Latent: a short vector standing for audio
steps.say: Every frame, three thousand two hundred samples of your voice go through the codec encoder and come out as sixty-four numbers. No codebook.
Those numbers are added to the model's last text token and its own last audio latent.
The sum is one position in the backbone, a four billion parameter language model.
Its output branches. A text head picks the next token. A small MeanFlow head turns noise into the next audio latent in one step.

scenes.credit: Higurashi technical blog, speech generation figure

steps.say: Compare Moshi-style codes. Each eighty millisecond frame is eight discrete codes, generated one after another by a second transformer.
Haru's frame is a single latent, and the flow head runs once. Fewer frames per second, and one pass each.

scenes.title: How fast, and how true
scenes.sub: The latency claim and the demo tracks
scenes.say: Chapter four. How fast, and how true?

scenes.title: From your last sound to its reply

steps.say: Say your last syllable. It lands somewhere inside a frame.
The model can't hear it until the frame completes. That's up to a hundred and thirty-three milliseconds, before any compute.
Then one model step. On an M one Max with int8 weights, the company measures thirty-four point two milliseconds.
With microphone, socket, output margin and headphones, the pipeline is sixty-five point two milliseconds. That's the headline.
Add the framing back, and the worst case is about a hundred and ninety-eight. Level with Moshi's two hundred, not ahead.

scenes.say: There is no turn-taking benchmark, but the demo videos keep each speaker on its own channel. Measured there, Haru takes the floor a fifth of a second after you stop.

steps.say: Here is the Japanese demo. Watch the playhead cross the mark for aizuchi, the short listening noises.
Then a stretch of overlapping talk. Both lanes busy at once, and neither one stops.

scenes.title: Where it is thin
scenes.say: The article found three soft spots.

items.say: There is no benchmark at all. No error rate, no turn-taking test, no comparison with Moshi.
The two-sided training audio was separated from single-track recordings, and separation is weakest exactly where people overlap.
And the sixty-five milliseconds leaves out the frame you wait for.
